title: Myanmar Verifies Nearly 309,000 Rohingya in Bangladesh but Delays Repatriation
excerpt: Myanmar's military government confirmed 308,797 displaced people as former Rakhine State residents but says returns will not begin until security conditions improve amid ongoing conflict with the Arakan Army.
body:
• Myanmar has verified 308,797 out of 828,824 names submitted by Bangladesh as former Rakhine State residents, its foreign ministry said.
  • Repatriation remains conditional on improved security in Rakhine, where the military is fighting the Arakan Army for territorial control.
  • Another 4,241 people on the list were flagged as linked to terrorist activities, while 113,507 could not be verified.
  • Human rights groups warn that conditions in northern Rakhine — including forced labour, movement restrictions, and armed conflict — make repatriation unsafe.

Verification Complete, Returns on Hold

Myanmar's military government has confirmed that nearly 309,000 displaced people living in camps in Bangladesh are former residents of Rakhine State, but repatriation will not proceed until security in the region improves, the country's foreign ministry said in a statement over the weekend.

https://x.com/PiQMarkets/status/2089200999479275864

Of the 828,824 names submitted by Bangladesh in six phases through July 31, 2026, Myanmar verified 308,797 individuals as former Rakhine residents, according to Reuters. The junta also identified 4,241 people on the repatriation list as involved in terrorist activities and said 113,507 could not be verified.

The verification marks a significant step in a process that has stalled repeatedly since 2017, when more than 700,000 Rohingya fled to neighbouring Bangladesh following a crackdown by Myanmar security forces that the United Nations described as conducted with "genocidal intent."

Conflict in Rakhine Blocks Return

The main obstacle to repatriation remains the ongoing armed conflict in Rakhine State between Myanmar's military and the Arakan Army, an ethnic armed group that has seized control of much of northern Rakhine, including the entire border with Bangladesh.

The Arakan Army launched a major offensive in November 2023 that drove the military out of large parts of the state. The fighting has displaced hundreds of thousands of civilians — both Rohingya and ethnic Rakhine — and cut off humanitarian access to wide swaths of the region.

Myanmar's foreign ministry said repatriation is "strictly a bilateral matter" with Bangladesh and that returns will begin only when conditions stabilize. Previous repatriation arrangements in 2018 and 2019 resulted in zero returnees despite bilateral preparations, underscoring the difficulty of the process.

Rights Groups Sound Alarm

Amnesty International has warned that conditions in northern Rakhine are "nowhere near ready for Rohingya to return safely." In a September 2025 report based on interviews with recently arrived refugees, the organization documented forced labour, severe movement restrictions, discriminatory livelihood bans, and inadequate access to healthcare and education under Arakan Army control.

"The Arakan Army has, to many Rohingya, replaced the Myanmar military as their oppressor."

— Joe Freeman, Amnesty International Myanmar Researcher

Refugees described being forced to carry construction materials to military checkpoints, clean up battlefield debris, and provide unpaid night guards — with beatings for those who refused. One interviewee said Arakan Army soldiers told Rohingya: "This is not your country. Get out of our country."

The World Food Programme reported in August 2025 that up to 57 percent of families in central Rakhine could not meet basic food needs, and said conditions in the north — where international organizations have no access — were likely "much worse."

Bangladesh Bears the Burden

Bangladesh currently hosts approximately 1.19 million forcibly displaced Rohingya, according to UNHCR data. The country's Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman told parliament in June 2026 that no timeline could be set for repatriation given the security situation.

Bangladesh has launched its Joint Response Plan Update 2026 seeking $710.5 million to support the refugee population, of which $291 million has been secured so far. Third-country resettlement has offered a limited outlet: 5,712 Rohingya have been resettled through the International Organization for Migration and 697 through the International Rescue Committee, with recent placements in Canada, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, and Australia.

Bangladesh has stressed that third-country resettlement is not a permanent solution and that safe, voluntary return to Rakhine remains the only durable answer.

Malaysia Deal Also in Limbo

Myanmar separately agreed to take back 5,000 Rohingya asylum seekers from Malaysia, but Malaysia said the repatriation will not proceed if lives are at risk — adding another stalled front to the crisis.

A UN General Assembly resolution on the Rohingya crisis, co-sponsored by 105 countries and jointly backed by the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the European Union, has called for stronger international efforts to ensure safe and dignified returns. But with active combat in Rakhine and no ceasefire in sight, the nearly one million Rohingya in Bangladesh face an indefinite wait.
nri_angle: The Rohingya refugee crisis has global implications, with resettlement programs placing refugees in countries including Canada, the UK, Australia, and New Zealand.
